summary:
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity and contains no provision criminalising a person for being transgender; same-sex relations have never been criminalised there. No instrument reviewed for this record creates such an offence at regional level either. The visitor-facing risk in the region is structural rather than statutory: it arises from which forum hears a dispute and which body of personal law applies, not from any provision aimed at gender non-conformity.

Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, whose drafting began on 29 March 2019, prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause commits the region to adjudication "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws", placing constitutional, religious and customary law side by side in the same adjudicative mandate.

On 14 July 2026 the Bangsamoro Parliament proposed a Shari'ah Justice System Code of 10 books that would extend Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status field confined to it since Presidential Decree 1083 of 1977, into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution. The proposal rests on the authority of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and on the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. Whether it has been enacted is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums, with written-opt-in clauses available to civil entities. This legal-pluralist marriage regime is the layer a visitor married to a Muslim spouse would encounter: the forum and the applicable personal law follow the religious status of the parties, not the visitor's own nationality.

In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, provinces of the Davao region, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; the Bangsamoro Parliament passed it unanimously. The measure carries the region's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing, so the forum questions above are no longer confined to Mindanao's autonomous area.
tangentialFactors:
The Shari'ah court system was confined to personal-status matters for Muslim Filipinos under Presidential Decree 1083 of 1977; the 2026 proposal would widen that mandate substantially, and the 2024 law widened its geographic reach. Both changes enlarge the set of disputes that could be heard outside ordinary civil courts.

The 2024 expansion was reported in November 2024 by Christianity Today with the reaction of local Christian leaders, indicating that the extension of Shari'ah jurisdiction is contested on religious grounds in the provinces it now reaches. That contest concerns institutional jurisdiction rather than any provision addressing gender identity.

For comparison, a 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 62 for trans travellers, in the 'Exercise Caution' band, with 81 for HIV-positive travellers. The Bangsamoro region draws no separate score in the sources reviewed, and the national figures should not be read as a measurement of conditions inside the autonomous region.

Nationally the protections available to a trans visitor are a patchwork: no SOGIE anti-discrimination statute is in force, the SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending since 2000, and protections sit in eight provincial and 32 city or municipal ordinances plus sectoral statutes. Whether any comparable ordinance exists within the Bangsamoro is not sourced here.
localsOnly:
Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13 sets out the governance structures of the autonomous region and guarantees religious freedom to its residents, while its justice clause binds the region to adjudicate in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, and traditional or tribal laws.

For Muslim residents of the region, marriage, divorce, succession and family relations are decided in Shari'ah forums under the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations, with written-opt-in provisions allowing civil entities to be brought into that regime.

The proposed Shari'ah Justice System Code, tabled in the Bangsamoro Parliament on 14 July 2026, would reorganise the Shari'ah justice system across 10 books and carry it into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution, rather than leaving it confined to the personal-status jurisdiction it has held since 1977.

Residents outside the autonomous region are also affected by the August 2024 statute creating three Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts in northern Mindanao, Davao-region provinces, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila, enacted with the unanimous support of the Bangsamoro Parliament.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses trans-specific legal status, document or marker rules, entry screening, facilities access, healthcare access or documented violence inside the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region. Whether any of the national findings on those subjects apply with particular force in the region is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the proposed Shari'ah Justice System Code of 14 July 2026 has been enacted, and in what final form, is unresolved in the sources reviewed; the inventory records the proposal only.

Whether the ta'tir offences or civil-action provisions contemplated by the 2026 proposal could reach gender non-conformity, cross-dressing or public presentation is not addressed by any source here and remains unresolved.

The inventory does not state whether regional or provincial ordinances within the Bangsamoro restrict cross-dressing or public presentation as some Philippine localities elsewhere do. No such ordinance is sourced for this region either way.

Local Christian-leader reaction to the 2024 Shari'ah court expansion is reported by a single religious publication; the depth and distribution of that reaction is not independently sourced.
